Chapter 7: The Culture Wars and the Politics of Blame
As we moved from the twentieth century into the twenty-first, the old lines drawn by class didn’t just disappear—they found brand new battlegrounds.
Suddenly, the so-called "culture wars"—these never-ending fights over values, identity, and who really belongs—became a favorite tool for politicians and pundits. Why? Because rallying supporters with emotional arguments was much easier than having honest conversations about deeper problems, like inequality.
Picture this: A mother working two jobs, just trying to keep her family going in a small town where the factory shut down years ago. She watches politicians on TV talking about “real Americans”—about who works hard, and who doesn’t. And sure, sometimes she might see a little bit of herself in those words. But most of the time? She just feels invisible. Or worse, like she’s being blamed for troubles she had no hand in creating.
The truth is, even though people didn’t talk about class out loud, it was always right there, just beneath the surface. Debates over things like school funding, healthcare, and taxes were often framed in a way that set groups against each other. Think about the stories you’ve heard: The “hardworking taxpayer” versus the “welfare cheat.” The “middle class” pitted against the “undeserving poor.” Most of us didn’t realize how these stories were shaping our views about who deserves help and who doesn’t.
And pop culture? It played its part too. Reality shows like “Here Comes Honey Boo Boo” or “Duck Dynasty” put the lives of rural, working-class white families under the spotlight. Sometimes these shows celebrated their resilience, but just as often, they blurred the line between entertainment and exploitation. The people at the center of those stories rarely got to share their own side.
Meanwhile, talk radio and cable news brought a whole new set of voices to the public conversation. But more often than not, those voices only deepened the old divides. Hosts railed against “elites” and “coastal snobs,” painting a picture of America split in two: the hardworking “real” folks versus the out-of-touch urbanites. If that sounds familiar, it should—it echoes old arguments about who gets to belong, and who doesn’t.
While all this was happening, the economy was transforming. Manufacturing jobs faded away, service work and gig jobs took over, and more and more people started to feel lost. The American Dream, once so close, now seemed farther away than ever. And that old story—about America being a classless society? It was getting harder to believe with each passing year.
In times like these, blame becomes a powerful weapon. Politicians and pundits pointed fingers at immigrants, at the poor—at anyone they could label as "other." The stigma of being poor and white never really left, but now it came with a new side of anger and betrayal. More and more people started to feel like the system was rigged against them—and honestly, they weren’t wrong.
The culture wars promised simple answers, but they’ve never really solved the real problems facing working-class and poor Americans. Those old class divisions? They’re still here, hidden in plain sight, quietly shaping lives and choices in ways most people never even notice.
